A mower that's running perfectly now might not be so cooperative after months in storage. A little preparation can help prevent costly surprises.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year. All you want to do is push that lawn mower into the shed and close and lock the door. But you can’t, and you’ll regret it if you do. Come the following spring, you’ll pull out a mower that is sluggish, with stale fuel, clogged carburetors, and broken parts. It’s entirely possible that that lawn mower won’t start in spring at all.

You can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance. It’s not as nice as tucking that mower away and drinking a cool beer, but it’s not all that difficult either. Once you learn how to winterize a lawn mower, you’ll find that it’s easier to jump in and do the work before you move your machine into winter storage.

I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest. Just follow this practical step-by-step approach. It won't take long if you tackle it alongside your other garden winterizing chores.

It only takes a month for the gasoline in a gas-powered motor to start to break down. When it does, it leaves gummy deposits in the carburetor. This doesn’t do anything good for the mower. You can tackle this in either of two ways.

First, and some would argue best, is to add a lawn mower fuel stabilizer to the remaining fresh gasoline in the tank. Sta-Bil, available on Amazon, is a good choice, but Sea Foam and Ethanol Shield are other popular options. But check your mower manufacturer's recommendations, as some don't advise this step.

To use a fuel stabilizer, first check the product instructions for the correct amount to add based on the gasoline volume. Add the stabilizer to the tank, then top up with fresh gasoline, leaving a little room for expansion. Run the engine for around 5-10 minutes, or as directed on the product label, to allow the treated fuel to circulate through the fuel system. This helps prevent gasoline from deteriorating during winter storage, reducing the risk of deposits forming in the carburetor and causing starting problems in spring.

The second option to winterize a gas mower is to empty the tank so that there is no gasoline to break down. You can do this easily by running the mower until it is totally out of gas. You can also empty the tank by draining the tank and carburetor bowl manually.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Before you start, switch off the engine, let it cool completely, and disconnect the spark plug wire for safety. If you need to tip the mower to access the underside, tilt it with the air filter and carburetor facing upward, as tipping it the wrong way can allow oil or fuel to leak into the air filter or engine intake.

Next, clean the underside of the mower, scraping away grass clippings and dirt with a plastic scraper or stiff nylon brush. Leaving damp debris in place over winter can cause corrosion on steel mower decks.

Once the underside is clean and completely dry, apply a protective coating. Mo-Deck Non-Stick Mower Deck Spray helps prevent grass clippings and debris from sticking to the deck, making cleanup easier when mowing season returns. Follow the product instructions and allow it to dry before storing the mower.

Draining the oil is not fun, but it’s not that difficult either. First, check your mower's manual, as some newer engines only require oil top-ups rather than regular changes. If yours needs an oil change, run the mower for a few minutes to warm the oil, then switch off the engine, let it cool enough to work safely, and disconnect the spark plug wire before proceeding.

Drain the old, dirty oil into a suitable container, following your mower's instructions. A Briggs & Stratton oil extractor kit makes the job much less messy, allowing you to remove oil through the fill tube without tipping the mower.

Does your mower have an oil filter? If so, change it now, using a replacement designed for your engine. Then refill with the correct amount of fresh motor oil. This will depend on your model, but common options include SAE 30 and synthetic 5W-30. Check the oil level with the dipstick to avoid overfilling, and take the used oil to a recycling facility.

Your lawn mower blade needs to be sharp and free of cracks. With the engine off and the spark plug wire disconnected, follow your mower's instructions to safely access and remove the blade. Wear thick gloves and check carefully for nicks, cracks, bends, or dull edges.

You can sharpen a dull blade with a hand file, but it's easier to use a proper lawn mower blade sharpener, like this Sporgain lawn mower blade sharpener and balancer from Amazon. However, if your lawn mower blade is cracked or badly damaged, it's better to replace it.

If you sharpen the blade yourself, follow the manufacturer's recommended angle and make sure it's properly balanced before reinstalling it. An unbalanced blade can cause excessive vibration and damage the mower.

At the same time, inspect the spark plug for wear, corrosion, or heavy carbon buildup. Remove it using a spark plug socket (this Milwaukee set from Home Depot has three sizes), and if the plug is damaged, badly worn, or heavily coated, it's best to replace it with a new one recommended for your mower. Otherwise, gently clean away any light buildup with a soft brush before putting it back. Check your mower's manual for any specific instructions.

The great thing about winterizing a battery-operated mower is that you don’t have to worry about gasoline issues. On the other hand, you do have to worry about looking after the battery. This is also important if your gasoline-powered mower has an electric starter.

Proper winter storage is essential. If the battery is removable, take it out of the mower and store it in a cool, dry place indoors, away from freezing temperatures and extreme heat. Check your manufacturer's recommendations for the ideal storage temperature, as requirements vary between batteries.

For lithium-ion batteries, most manufacturers recommend storing them partially charged, rather than fully charged or empty. Check the charge periodically throughout winter and top it up if needed.

However, if your mower uses a lead-acid battery, you generally need to keep it fully charged during storage. A compatible battery maintainer can help prevent them from going flat. The Noco Genius1 Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer maintains the battery's charge throughout winter so it's ready to go when mowing season returns. Do make sure any charger or maintainer you use is suitable for your battery type.

Move your mower into a dry shed, garage, or other sheltered space where it will be protected from rain, snow, and ice. Ideally, keep it on a clean, dry surface, as sitting on damp ground over winter can cause rust and corrosion.

A breathable, water-resistant lawn mower cover, like this Himal Outdoors Push Lawn Mower Cover from Amazon, is a good idea because it helps keep dust, dirt, and moisture off the mower when it's not in use. Make sure the mower is completely cool and dry before covering it.

Avoid storing your mower near corrosive household chemicals, fertilizers, or pool chlorine, as their fumes or spills can damage metal components over time. If you're storing it in a garage or shed, leave enough space around the machine for ventilation and easy access.

It's easy to recreate the look in your own garden with beautiful white roses – and November is the perfect time to plant.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there's one thing Miley Cyrus knows how to do, it's make a statement. And her recent wedding to musician Maxx Morando has given us plenty of inspiration – particularly when it comes to the flowers.

The couple's romantic ceremony featured masses of beautiful white roses, with a breathtaking floral arch creating a dreamy backdrop for the celebrations. It's classic, understated and wonderfully romantic. And, honestly? We're already dreaming about recreating the look in our own backyards. The good news is that November is one of the best times to get started. Bare-root roses are coming into season, making this the perfect opportunity to plant your own romantic rose display – often for considerably less than you'd spend on established container-grown plants.

So, while Miley might have had a team of florists to bring her wedding vision to life, you can take a slightly more long-term approach. Plant now, give your roses time to establish over winter, and you could be enjoying your own beautiful floral display come spring and summer. After all, as Miley herself once reminded us, we can absolutely buy ourselves flowers. But growing them ourselves? Even better.

There's something wonderfully timeless about an all-white flower display. While colorful planting schemes certainly have their place, sticking to one color can create a much more elegant look – and white roses, as Miley Cyrus' wedding photos have proven, are particularly lovely for this.

The beauty of this look is that you don't need hundreds of individual plants to make an impact. A well-positioned rose bush, a climbing variety trained over an arch or trellis, or even a small collection of white roses along a garden path can create a n atmosphere that's just as romantic.

Better still? Well, there's no need to wait until spring to start planning your own rose garden, because November is actually the ideal time to get planting. Bare-root roses become available from late fall and are generally much more affordable than their container-grown counterparts, making them a brilliant option if you're hoping to plant several together.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you're looking for something that combines good looks with wildlife appeal, this shrub rose produces fragrant white blooms, followed by ornamental rose hips that provide additional seasonal interest.

For something a little closer to the full-bodied blooms seen at Miley's wedding, this floribunda variety produces gorgeous double white blooms, sometimes with the faintest blush of pink.

Of course, if it's the dramatic floral arch you're hoping to recreate, you'll want to consider a climbing rose. This pretty variety is ideal for training over arches, pergolas and trellises.

The good news? You don't need an elaborate wedding installation to achieve that same Miley Cyrus-inspired look; you just need a sturdy garden arch like this pergola from Outsunny, and pop it somewhere that gets plenty of sunlight. (Most roses need at least six hours of direct sunlight each day).

Next, plant a climbing rose on either side of your structure, allowing the canes to grow and training them horizontally and upwards as they develop. Be patient, though, as your rose arch won't become an overnight sensation, and it may take a couple of growing seasons to achieve the look you're craving.

And there you have it: a little celebrity-inspired garden magic without the celebrity price tag. Miley Cyrus' wedding might have lasted just one day, but with the right roses and a little patience, you can enjoy your own romantic floral display year after year. Talk about a love story worth growing, eh?

#7901. The Best Waterproof Gloves of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 21, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Like a rain jacket for your hands, waterproof gloves are essential gear for those working—or playing—outdoors in cold or inclement weather. For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

We searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

We initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

In our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester says: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Carhartt waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Women on the hunt for warm, waterproof gloves may want to look at MCTi’s ski gloves. They pair a polyurethane outer shell with a faux leather palm and thumb-grip area for holding ski poles or other slippery objects. On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. Not only that, but the insulation was less puffy than some of the other gloves we tested, which improved dexterity and flexibility for gripping and handling small items. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

Get the MCTi waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Men looking for lightweight protection from the weather may want to consider Ozero’s men’s thermal gloves, which provide warmth and weather resistance without a lot of bulk. These gloves feature a water-resistant and windproof polyester construction that keeps the wearer’s hands dry and warm in inclement weather (most of the shell fabric is indeed waterproof, but the seams and touch-screen pads on two fingers are not, hence the “water-resistant” designation). This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Also note that these gloves cost less than most of the others we tested. Moreover, they are slim and flexible and easily fit into jacket pockets.

Get the Ozero waterproof gloves at Amazon or Walmart.

Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. Youngstown Glove Company’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade quickly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Get the Youngstown waterproof gloves at Amazon, JB Tools, or Youngstown Glove Company.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

No more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an important text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. We appreciated that they were truly 100 percent waterproof, both in our simulated rain test and when immersed in water. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

These gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That said, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

Built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

Get the Hestra Titan waterproof gloves at Amazon.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

#7900. Shrubs Steal the Show in Bonnie’s Colorado Garden

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:

Colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

#7899. Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

If you see evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips in late fall or early winter, it's a sure sign you need to protect plants from frost, freezing temperatures and cold winds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is important so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:

If the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

There are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

Your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

During a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing new, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

Some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

Desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

Distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from new foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the issue, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

Evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

First – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

Now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

If those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

Next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

Now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

These steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s important not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger new growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

Wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout new growth.

Keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:

Dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic issue, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

#7898. Crucial Snow Blower Maintenance Tasks to Complete Before the First Snow

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 21, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

Spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”

In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:

Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s important to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”

Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

To change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” says Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”

If these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, says Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

Designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, says Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

“A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

Would a mini greenhouse or a cold frame be best for your garden needs this winter? Here's everything you need to know to decide…

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

Most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

Cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

Plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

So, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to quickly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

When buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

When buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

Look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

Double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

Reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

It's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick big bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

If you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

Whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

#7892. Connie’s Garden in Griffin, Georgia

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Griffin, Georgia, for an update from Connie Raines. We first visited Connie’s garden shortly after she moved into her new home and transplanted many of her plants. Now, a little over a year later, she’s back with a few highlights from spring and late summer. Here’s Connie:

I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual)

Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias

Perennial begonia (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9), a soft mahonia bush just planted this spring, and amaranth

A watermelon my husband grew in our garden area created by a new stepped retaining wall.

A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

This celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

Thanks for sharing another update from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂

#7891. The Best Carpet Cleaners of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Amber Guetebier, Michelle Larson, Debbie Wolfe, Additional research provided by Timothy Dale

Published Nov 23, 2026 8:17 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

For an active household with lots of foot or paw traffic, a carpet cleaner, sometimes called a carpet shampooer, can make quick work of cleaning common stains and refreshing dingy rugs or carpets. Whether you’ve considered one for spot cleaning or need more frequent whole-house cleaning, carpet cleaners can make upkeep a lot easier.

We tested 23 top-rated carpet cleaners on rugs, carpets, and stairs to find which ones leave flooring fibers looking like new while also offering the best value. Our favorite was the Hoover SmartWash+ Automatic Carpet Cleaner thanks to its effective stain removal and overall cleaning power. Read on to find out why we also consider the following to be some of the best carpet cleaners on the market and learn about what features will best suit your home and lifestyle.

Whether you’re looking for a portable option for quick spot-cleaning or an upright for whole-house cleaning, our list has you covered. See how each carpet and rug cleaner we recommend fared in our tests and which one might be best for your needs.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

With no buttons to push or triggers to pull, Hoover’s high-tech SmartWash+ carpet cleaner makes quick and easy work of messy tasks. Pushing the unit forward automatically turns on the cleaning function, and pulling it back switches the machine to auto-dry. The cleaner’s AutoMix system combines and dispenses the correct amount of carpet cleaner solution​, while the 1-gallon tank provides ample capacity for washing and rinsing.

In testing, it only took a few passes to remove all the test stains from our carpet square and get it bone dry. We found the dry-only mode especially helpful—so much so that we even used it on a couple of other still-wet test squares and pulled out an impressive amount of excess moisture. In addition to being easy to use and effective, this upright carpet-cleaning machine was lighter than similar models, which made it easier to maneuver and carry. With its longer power cord, 8-foot hose, and several attachments (including one for pet hair), it’s also quite versatile.

The downsides of this otherwise great machine were build quality and a not-always-intuitive design. Some plastic pieces came loose when we removed the hose, and we struggled to get them back into place. Also, after we took off the brush and cover for cleaning, they weren’t super easy to snap back on. Still, those issues felt minor compared to the overall value of this very effective carpet cleaner.

What our tester says: “It took us a little while to get used to the lack of buttons and triggers, but once we used the machine for a bit, we found it to be one of our favorites.”—Amber Guetebier, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Hoover SmartWash+ carpet cleaner at Amazon or Target.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 5/5; Suction 4.5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4/5

This budget-friendly Hoover model is a whole-home carpet cleaner with a user-friendly compact design. It weighs just 12.5 pounds, making it ideal for anyone with limited storage space, yet the 0.5-gallon tank provides enough water for most rooms. This unit also features Hoover’s HeatForce Technology, which heats the carpet as dirty water is sucked into the tank for faster drying. It comes with a pet brush roll that helps collect hair and purge difficult stains, and though it doesn’t have a hose attachment, its low profile lets users get under furniture fairly easily.

This compact upright cleaner impressed us with how quickly it removed carpet stains, eliminating them in three passes, which took less than 5 minutes. After running it for another 2 minutes without dispensing any more water, our carpet square was dry to the touch. Though it was fast and very easy to use, the fact that it doesn’t come with an attachment hose made getting into small spaces and corners a little difficult. Also, compared to others, the process of removing the dirty water was a little awkward, but not enough to be a deal-breaker, especially at this price point. If you’re in the market for a carpet cleaner machine that gets the job done with no fuss and at a great price, this is an excellent choice.

Get the Hoover PowerDash carpet cleaner at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Effectiveness 4.3/5; Suction 5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4.7/5

The Bissell Little Green portable carpet and upholstery cleaner is a versatile machine designed to tackle everything from stained carpets to sticky auto interiors. Its powerful suction capabilities can efficiently remove messes from almost any soft surface, yet it’s small enough to carry from place to place without any hassle. The Little Green comes with two 48-ounce water tanks (one for clean water and one for dirty) that are easy to remove and maintain, a 3-inch tough-stain tool, a HydroRinse attachment, and a sample-size bottle of the brand’s cleaning solution.

In testing, this carpet spot cleaner​ easily eliminated dirt and fresh stains, and it greatly improved the appearance of set-in stains. We liked its large-capacity tanks, which reduced the frequency of filling and emptying, as well as its lightweight build and 15-foot cord for portability. And given how much of a pain it typically is to clean the hoses on carpet cleaners, the HydroRinse self-cleaning tool made it much easier to get the job done without spilling water everywhere.

Read our full review: Bissell Little Green Portable Carpet Cleaner

Get the Bissell Little Green carpet cleaner at Amazon, Ace Hardware, The Home Depot, Wayfair, or Bissell.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Suction 4/5; Portability 4.5/5; Value 4.6/5

With its low price and solid performance, Kenmore’s RevitaLite portable carpet cleaner gave our best bang for the buck winner a run for its money. However, given this budget-friendly model’s light weight and incredibly long hose and cord, it’s an easy win for the best carpet cleaner for stairs. Whether you’re in need of whole-house or spot cleaning, it does an excellent job removing everyday dirt as well as set-in stains.

In testing, this lightweight carpet cleaner​ was one of the easiest upright models to push and pull, likely because its clean and dirty water tanks sit quite low on the unit. Even with the 3.2-liter water tank full, it weighed just over 25 pounds, which helped a lot when maneuvering around furniture feet and up stairs.

While it only comes with two tools (a 3.5-inch tough stain tool and a 6.5-inch wide path tool), we found they were enough for everything from pulling up pet messes to getting old stains out of couch pillows. If we had one complaint, it’s that it didn’t seem to pull out as much extra moisture as others, which left the carpet a bit damp. A storage mat would be nice for catching post-cleaning drips, but for the price, it’s really a pretty minor issue.

Before we began testing, we researched more than three dozen products, ranging from small portable options to professional-style equipment and even a few steam carpet cleaners. We considered weight, cord length, and accessories, and we also looked at carpet cleaner reviews to determine what made potential picks exceptional.

We then tested 23 different carpet cleaners on a carpet swatch marked by several tough-to-clean stains, including red wine, chocolate, dirt, and oil. We also used them around the house on old stains and furniture when possible, trying all included accessories, carrying each machine up and down stairs, and monitoring how long the carpet took to dry after use. We then rated each machine on how quickly and how well it eliminated stains, overall ease of use, portability, and suction, and assigned our favorite models awards based on their strengths.

Carpet cleaning equipment often features various cleaning modes and includes several accessories. Hose and cord length affect how long the unit can continuously clean before unplugging and moving. Keeping these factors in mind when shopping can help ensure you pick the best residential carpet cleaner for your needs.

Spot-cleaning machines are lightweight, portable, and less expensive than whole-house cleaners, but their suction isn’t as strong as larger units. A handheld carpet cleaner is ideal for use on stairs, in homes with just a couple of carpeted rooms, or on area rugs. These small carpet cleaners are also good for cleaning the carpets in the car.

Whole-house or upright carpet cleaners have robust motors, powerful suction, and thick, rotating brushes that provide deep cleaning. Many models offer multiple cleaning modes and use their own cleaning solutions, making them better suited to larger homes with many carpeted rooms that see heavy traffic. A whole-house, heavy-duty carpet cleaner is ideal for lifting dirt and grime that’s settled deep into carpet or rug fibers.

Buyers will want to consider their physical limits, the amount of carpeting, and the number of levels in the home when making a decision. In general, the heavier the machine, the more powerful its suction motor and rotating brushes will be. Portable carpet cleaners, like handheld carpet cleaners, are lighter and easier to maneuver, whereas full-size upright machines capable of heavy-duty cleaning will be harder to move and store.

Cord and hose length both affect cleaning time; the less often you have to unplug and plug in, the more efficient the cleaning session. Long cords of 20 feet or more and hoses up to 10 feet are particularly helpful in large rooms and for cleaning stairs. Since some upright units don’t have hoses, buyers wanting to clean under heavy pieces of furniture will want to be careful when choosing.

Carpet-cleaner accessories are attachments that can be added to a hose or intake port for cleaning different materials, reaching difficult areas, or dealing with pet hair and odors. Some of the most common types include upholstery cleaners; crevice-cleaning attachments (handy for tight spots like the indent created where the baseboard meets the carpet); or spinning brushes that lift tough, stuck-on stains. Pet attachments include special brushes, guards, and even isolated tanks for trapping fur to prevent it from getting caught in the machine. Many machines include samples of the brand’s best carpet shampoos or cleaning solutions to help you start cleaning right away.

Before buying or renting a carpet cleaner to keep your carpet looking new, take a look at these frequently asked questions and their answers.

The price range in this lineup is $125 to $700. However, the average cost of hiring a professional carpet cleaner is about $50 per room and can be up to $600 for larger homes. This means that after just a few uses, your new carpet cleaner will have paid for itself. You also have the option of renting carpet-cleaning equipment and DIYing the job at an average price of $30 per day. Either of these routes may make sense if you have just one or two carpeted rooms, but if your entire house is carpeted or you live with small children or furry friends, it may be more cost-effective to compare carpet cleaners and invest in your own unit.

If regular vacuuming and moderate care are taken, a carpet can be cleaned once every 12 to 18 months. In an active household with pets and children, you’ll want to clean the carpet every 6 to 12 months.

The best carpet cleaner for pets can remove pet hair, odors, and stains from even the deepest fibers of the carpet. In our tests, the Shark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet With StainStriker did a great job on these tasks as well as on more serious pet messes.

Bissell recommends staying off carpet for 4 to 6 hours after cleaning, but total dry time depends on a variety of factors, including the type of carpet fibers, the pile, how much solution and water were used, room size, ventilation, humidity, and temperature. Carpet made from polyester takes between 6 and 12 hours to dry, but wool carpet takes at least 24 hours to dry. To reduce drying time, use a quick-cleaning mode, which releases less liquid, and increase ventilation by opening windows, turning on fans, and turning on heat or air conditioning.

If you want to remove surface stains or odors, shampooing your carpets will be better. To deep clean and sanitize carpet, a steam cleaner will be more effective.

How much you should spend on a carpet cleaner depends on your needs regarding features, size, and frequency of use. The carpet cleaners selected for this guide cost between $125 and $700, which reflects the typical price range for reliable models.

#7889. Autumn in a Montana Garden

Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

The back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

An ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

The narrow gap at the bottom of a closed garage door is more than enough space for dirt, leaves, blowing snow, and rain to find their way inside, making a mess of your garage. Mice, rats, roaches, and other pests can also use this opening for easy access to your garage—and even to your home if you have an attached garage. However, a simple remedy for keeping out the elements and reducing the likelihood of pest infestations is a garage door threshold.

The best garage door threshold is typically made with a cushioned rubber or vinyl top and may feature an aluminum frame to install the seal to the bottom of a garage door. Based on our research, the Jin&Bao Universal Garage Door Threshold Seal Strip is our favorite for its weatherproof construction, temperature resistance, and easy installation. This guide will explore the most important factors to consider as you shop for this handy item and offer a look at some of the top products on the market to properly seal your garage.

Bottom line: Garage door thresholds are essential for protecting your garage from weather, debris, and pests, with top picks offering durability and easy installation.

The best garage door threshold can protect the flooring of a garage while keeping valuables secure and free of damage from water, debris, and pests. The top picks feature a selection of these versatile products in a variety of categories chosen with overall quality, price, and the above-mentioned considerations in mind.

For a watertight seal that lasts in any weather conditions, rely on the Jin&Bao universal garage door threshold seal strip. This option has a weatherproof construction that keeps the garage clean by preventing water, dirt, snow, dust, and leaves from coming in and withstands temperatures of -40 to 280 degrees Fahrenheit. Plus, the construction will never warp, crack, or dry out with use, so it will last in any garage threshold for years.

This option is 20 feet long by 3.7 inches wide by 0.6 inch high and is available in three colorways: green, yellow, and blue. The anti-slip ridges also keep tires in place while you’re driving over them and prevent slips and falls; the grooved base provides adhesion to the sealant on concrete, asphalt, and painted or treated garage floors. All in all, this pick is a reliable option for those who want to keep grime and dust out of their garages, making it ideal for wooded areas, garage workshops, or for those who have tractors, bikes, or trucks coming in and out.

Get the Jin&Bao garage door threshold at Amazon.

This garage door threshold from CloudBuyer measures 0.5 inches in height, 3.5 inches in width, and about 10 feet in length, though every threshold is made slightly longer to ensure the length is sufficient after customizing for the specific garage door opening. It’s easy to cut the threshold with a sharpened utility knife because it’s made with a flexible, nontoxic rubber material.

Once installed, the threshold creates a watertight seal that prevents water, snow, dust, dirt, and leaves from entering the garage. The rubber withstands extreme temperatures and won’t crack, dry out, break, or shift after installation. The garage door threshold doesn’t include the adhesive, so it will need to be purchased prior to installation.

Get the CloudBuyer garage door threshold at Amazon.

Rainwater can seep into a garage and cause damage to the tools and materials inside. Especially during winter weather, standing water in a garage may freeze and can lead to cracks in the poured concrete floor. To help prevent damage to the garage and its contents, this eco-PVC rubber garage door threshold from Weather Defender seals out water, snow, ice, and freezing winds that can drive these elements indoors. It also keeps out leaves, dust and debris, and pests like rats, mice, and snakes.

This garage door bottom seals to the floor with a grooved base, creating an ideal surface for the included adhesive. This universal garage door threshold from Papillon is 20 feet long, and it’s easy to customize with a utility knife for a perfect fit along the entire length of the garage door opening. The rubber threshold is 3.5 inches wide and 0.5 inches in height, preventing leaves, dirt, grass, rain, snow, snakes, and rodents from invading the garage.

The EPDM rubber is designed to withstand extreme cold and hot temperatures. The quality of the weatherproof seal doesn’t shift, crack, or dry out with temperature fluctuations, enabling it to reduce the corrosion and rust that can be caused by pooling and freezing water. The garage is susceptible to infestations from insects, rodents, and snakes. With a garage door threshold, the gap between the garage door and the floor can be completely sealed ensuring snow, water, and frigid wind—much less a variety of critters—cannot penetrate the space. This durable vinyl garage door threshold from M-D Building Products helps insulate the garage when the door is down, slowing the transfer of heat through the door.

This garage door threshold is easy to install. The silicone adhesive is included, so it only needs to be measured, cut, and laid; no need to run out to purchase adhesive. Garage door threshold seals look pretty similar when held up side by side, so we looked at specific features to identify the best options. Available lengths and the ability to trim the strip to size were the first critical features. We excluded thresholds made with materials that were inflexible or insufficiently waterproof.

The materials used in the best seals, from eco-PVC to natural rubber to EPDM rubber, each feature different temperature resistance and a different type of deal to garage door bottom seals. A particularly important criteria for making this list was the ability to get a good seal between the threshold and the garage flooring; extra grooves to allow glue to spread out helps, and often it’s helpful when the threshold manufacturer includes their preferred adhesive right inside the package.

Finally, while the cosmetic appearance of a garage threshold is less important than the function, visibility strips provide safety, and for some homeowners, the option of matching the threshold to the color of the existing floor is a deciding factor.

Few situations can ruin a day faster than walking to the garage in the morning to find that a late-night rainstorm has completely flooded it, ruining tools and materials in the process. To help avoid this problem, as well as issues with blowing debris and pest infestations, choose a garage door threshold that has the proper size proportions for the garage opening, watertight protection, and a soft but durable construction that will secure the garage without damaging the door through regular use. Keep reading to learn more about these and other important factors to consider when choosing the best garage door threshold.

Determine the necessary height of the garage door threshold by measuring the gap between the bottom of the garage door and the garage floor when the door is closed. To ensure that the measurements are accurate for the entire length of the gap, take measurements at semi-regular intervals.

After finding the correct height, look for a suitable garage door threshold that will fit the space while forming a tight, waterproof seal. For homes that have frequent problems with standing rainwater and storms, investing in a taller threshold is recommended. By installing this taller threshold slightly away from the garage door, it still creates a seal while allowing the door to close easily.

The required length of the garage door threshold is easy to measure. Just use a tape measure to determine the length of the garage door opening and look for a product that is slightly longer. This extra length ensures that the threshold can be customized to the specific garage door to form a watertight seal.

Typically, a garage door threshold ranges from 10 to 20 feet in length. To achieve the desired length for a specific garage, the soft rubber or vinyl can be cut with a utility knife. A threshold with an aluminum base can be customized with a hacksaw. However, instead of a single 20-foot piece of aluminum that must be cut to size, these products usually include several short aluminum strips for use as needed.

The best garage door threshold is constructed with waterproof material designed to protect the garage from dust, debris, and pests. The material is intended to be flexible for two reasons: One, so the garage door isn’t damaged when it closes, and two, so the door forms a tight seal with the garage floor to block rain, dirt and debris, and pests from entering the garage.

Common materials used to make a garage door threshold include aluminum, rubber, and vinyl. Aluminum creates a durable, stiff frame that resists shifting and can be secured to the bottom of the garage door. Rubber and vinyl are both the primary materials to make the threshold seal. These materials are waterproof, flexible, and durable, so they can withstand the weight of the garage door while keeping out water, dirt, and pests.

The purpose of a garage door threshold is to protect the garage itself and all the tools, appliances, vehicles, and other valuables contained inside. This generally refers to keeping rainwater, standing water, or melting snow from running into the garage and flooding the floor, but protection doesn’t stop there.

The best garage door threshold can also act as a physical barrier that prevents leaves, dirt, and other debris from being blown into the garage. Additionally, the seal can keep out pests, like mice, rats, snakes, and roaches, while helping to insulate the garage from outdoor temperatures. This simple device secures the garage, creating a more pleasant place to store items and work on projects.
