#7819. Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra Review: Nearly Perfect Pool Cleaning

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 25, 2026 8:07 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models. I ran it through repeated cleaning cycles in my 8,500-gallon saltwater pool in Florida, where leaves, bugs, fine debris, and the occasional patch of algae give pool robots plenty to deal with. Setup was super simple: The Aiper app connected quickly, the robot updated without any fuss, and I had it in the water about 15 minutes after opening the box.

What impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle. Plenty of the robotic pool cleaners we’ve tested at Bob Vila handle floors, walls, and the waterline, but only a select few can also skim floating debris from the surface. That matters in my open-air pool, which regularly collects bugs and leaves. Anything the Aiper actually reaches gets cleaned extremely well.

The MicroMesh filter is another highlight. It traps extremely fine material, including algae and sediment that can slip through coarser filter baskets. Cleaning that ultra-fine layer takes a little more effort—I usually spend a few minutes thoroughly rinsing it with a hose and then leave it out to dry—but that’s a fair trade-off for how much fine material it captures. The app is also among the better pool-cleaner apps I’ve used, and I like getting a notification when the cleaning cycle is finished. The robot then floats neatly near the pool edge for retrieval.

Where the V3 Ultra disappointed me was its claim of shallow-area cleaning. Aiper says it can work in water down to about 7.9 inches deep, but my sun shelf is apparently too shallow for it to clean reliably. I still have to brush debris from the shelf into the main pool and let the robot collect it there. It also won’t clean my pool steps. For a $2,300 machine marketed around near-total pool coverage, those are significant omissions—especially since sun shelves have become so common in newer pools.

Still, I’m a fan of the Scuba V3 Ultra overall. My older Aiper cleaner has been running reliably for close to two years, which gives me more confidence in the brand than I’d have from a short-term test alone. The voice assistant is useful without being obnoxious, retrieval is simple, filtration is excellent, and cleaning performance everywhere the robot can reach is phenomenal. I’m still waiting for the robot that will truly clean every inch of my pool, but the Scuba V3 Ultra gets closer than most.

If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA

The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON

“For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD

“Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a new sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD

“Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER

“Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON

“I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two new bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON

“Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can quickly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ

“Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN

“Alphabetizing spices helps you quickly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND

“When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART

“For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT

“A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE

“My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON

“Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER

“A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI

“If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the new filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT

“An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI

“When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER

Hardwood floors are a coveted classic for their diverse graining and beautiful colors that add richness and dimension to so many decor schemes. But in homes with children, pets, and/or heavy traffic, hardwood floors are prone to showing dirt and dust quickly.

If maintained properly—and that means having the right tool—wood flooring can hold its finish for years without damage or cracking. Some brooms, for instance, can be too abrasive, whereas mops designed to clean hardwood floors are ideal for these surfaces.

It can be tricky to pick a floor mop that suits your cleaning style and budget, as well as the degree of dirt and stains on your flooring. Our top pick, Mr. Siga Professional Microfiber Mop for Wood Floors, was easy to use and cleaned our floors quickly and thoroughly. To help you find the best mop for your situation, we put a host of different products through their paces in a home with plenty of dust, dirt, and pet hair. We also spoke to professionals like Ryan Knoll, owner of Tidy Casa in Scottsdale, Arizona, to get a bit of expert knowledge on what shoppers will want to look for in a mop. Read on to see what to look for in the best mops for wood floors, as well as our reviews of products we deem superior in today’s crowded market.

Bottom line: Discover the best mops for wood floors, tested for performance and ease of use, to keep your hardwood looking pristine.

Many do not know what to look for in the best mops for hardwood floors, but here are some real-life reviews to get you started. Check out the following models, all of which met our criteria for quality, ease of use, and overall performance, to find the best mops for wood flooring for your particular needs.

The very wide rectangular mophead with a 360-degree swivel action meant less work on large hardwood floors, since with fewer swipes and greater maneuverability, we got our dusting and wet-mopping jobs done quickly.

At first, we were stumped on how to moisten the cleaning cloth, but a bit of online research taught us a few tricks for microfiber mops. Simply wet the cloth, roll it up to wring it out, then attach it to the mophead base. The microfiber mop cloths are reusable—just toss in the washing machine to launder. A handy dirt scrubber attachment is included for tight corners and tough grime, and the mop can be used on a variety of surfaces, including marble, tile, and laminate, as well as hardwood.

What our tester says: “This pick’s wide, swiveling mophead helped us clean large floors with fewer passes, and the adjustable handle made it easy to reach under furniture.”—Stephanie Cronk, Product Reviews tester and writer

For those who are looking for an effective way to clean hardwood floors all in one step, a vac/mop combo may be the answer.

The Tineco Floor ONE S5 smart wet/dry vacuum cleaner is an all-in-one machine. The unit vacuums up debris while mopping the floor simultaneously. It is self-propelled, which makes cleaning a breeze, especially anyone with arm or back issues.

Steam mopping offers a floor-cleaning solution that eliminates 99.9 percent of germs and bacteria without leaving behind any toxic residue. The O-Cedar ProMist Max Microfiber Spray Mop seemed promising with its unique wraparound flat mophead (akin to a mitten on the base of the mop). But in practice, it absorbed liquid (including its own cleaning fluid) poorly, and merely smeared dirt and dried ketchup around. We wanted to like its lightweight design, but it felt cheap and flimsy, particularly the trigger-spray handle.

We put a series of mops for hardwood floors, both cordless and corded, through their paces in a typical home that accumulated dust, dirt, pet hair, and muddy paw prints. We used the mops with their provided cleaners or distilled water, as recommended by the manufacturers.

We noted how easy or difficult the mops were to assemble, and considered the practicality of storing them. Finally, we used each in a controlled test of dried mud and ketchup smeared on hardwood floors and noted how much mess each floor mop left behind.

When purchasing a mop for wood flooring, think about its ease of use, any cleaning solutions it dispenses, and the price. In addition to the tool itself, factor in the size of the area that needs mopping. Here are some important considerations to look at when looking at mops for wood floors.

There are different types of mops available to suit various floor-maintenance preferences: flat mops, string mops, steam mops, and dust mops. Some are used exclusively for dusting floors, while other kinds function as both wet and dry mops.

Old-fashioned dunk-in-a-bucket mops require hand-wringing, but there are more convenient, less-messy options today. These mops may feature electric or mechanical components for wringing, as well as either reusable or disposable parts, so look for the type and system that suits your cleaning preference, floor type, and floor size.

The business end of a floor mop is typically either disposable or reusable. Disposable options are convenient for quick touch-ups and smaller floors, while reusable ones often prove more budget-friendly and can tackle larger surfaces.

Both types of mopheads impact sustainability, but in different ways. Reusable mopheads require water and chemicals to launder after use, while disposable versions head straight to the landfill. For larger areas, a reusable, machine-washable mophead is probably more efficient and eco-friendly than using multiple disposable mopheads per cleaning session. Those who prefer a reusable option might consider microfiber mopheads, which will catch and hold dirt and liquids better than materials such as cotton or sponge while reducing the look of scratches and scuffs.

According to Knoll, “Microfiber is the go-to. It’s soft, absorbent, and won’t damage your floors. It also wrings out well, keeping the water usage minimal.” He also added that microfiber mops are “great for picking up dust and fine particles without leaving scratches.”

If pushing a manual mop around seems laborious and inefficient, consider an electric model. These products typically have a variety of cleaning modes and processes (including one specifically for wood floors), and may feature the use of steam and/or cleaning solutions. They often come with swiveling heads for easier maneuverability, too.

Electric mops may be corded or cordless—and both types require access to an outlet. Corded mops must be plugged in during use, while the battery charger of cordless models must be plugged in as well. The portability of cordless models tends to appeal to folks who don’t want to be tied down to the length of a cord, typically because they have large areas to clean, and sometimes on different levels.

When stubborn dirt and stains occur, wood floors may require more vigorous cleaning than just dry-mopping, but only with a product specifically formulated for hardwood flooring. While hardwood floors are usually finished and sealed, some versions may be unsealed—it’s important to avoid using water on unsealed hardwood floors, as well as harsh cleansers on any wood floor. An all-purpose floor cleaner, for instance, may dull or, worse, strip the finish.

Though there are different types of cleaning solutions, those that can be used straight from the container without diluting tend to be safer, since any excess water from mixing a concentrated formula can seep into the wood and damage it. Some mops employ steam to clean and sanitize flooring, which should be safe for sealed hardwood—but to be safe, consult and follow all directions to avoid damage.

Knoll recommends gentle cleaners: “Opt for pH-neutral, hardwood-specific cleaners to prevent damage.” Also, “damp mopping is the way. Ensure the mop is just moist enough to clean without leaving excess water.”

When it comes to mopping around furniture, under beds/sofas, and into hard-to-reach areas, maneuverability matters. A swivel-head mop is ideal for getting around obstacles. The shape of the mophead (circular, triangular, or rectangular) also impacts how easily it can access corners and tight spots.

Mops may also include ergonomic features, some of which affect maneuvering, like telescoping handles to adjust length, and thereby extend reach. A poorly designed handle can also lead to arm and hand fatigue, so users will want to look for a model with a grip that feels good.

Those who still want more information on cleaning hardwood flooring with a quality mop may find it here in the answers to some of the most common questions about this household chore.

Mopping correctly can be a great way to maintain hardwood flooring, but using the wrong cleaning products can actually damage these expensive surfaces. A damp mop is often all that’s required to clean a hardwood floor; if the mop is too wet (with water or cleaning solution), excess liquid can seep into the cracks, causing the wood to warp.

Cleaning a floor starts with removing dust and debris by sweeping, vacuuming, or dry-mopping. For stubborn dirt and stains, use a cleaner designed for the specific floor material, using a “less is more” approach according to the manufacturer’s directions. To mop a floor correctly, dip string or sponge mops in the cleaning fluid, wring it out, and then swab with the damp mop. Use plain water to do a final rinse if desired. Start mopping in a far corner of the room, moving in the direction of the grain on hardwood floors, and work your way to the door. When finished, rinse the mop and let it air dry or wash any reusable pads.

Swiffer’s heavy-duty pads are considered safe for linoleum, vinyl, laminate, and ceramic tile, as well as sealed wood, marble, and stone. They should not be used on unsealed wood floors. As with all floor cleaners, be cautious using any fluid on unfinished, damaged, or especially delicate materials.

The National Wood Flooring Association recommends a heavy-duty mopping on wood floors monthly with a wood-flooring cleaner. However, it is safe to dry-mop daily or do a light mop on high-traffic areas once a week. For those without children and pets, feel free to give a very light mop on light-traffic areas more often.

#7816. The Reason Some Parking Lots Have Angled Spaces Instead of Straight Ones

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”

Back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

#7815. 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice quickly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products.  “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

#7813. Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:

[W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed new limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing new terms for future cooperation in any event….

[But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a new state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "issue orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

We also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

Testing workbenches can be a lot of fun, and we did our best to truly put these models through the paces.

First, we assessed assembly and setup. We wanted to make sure that each bench was really as portable as it claims. We set them up, broke them down, and moved them around to assess their weight and ease of use. Next, we set them up and used each of them as a miter saw stand and grinding surface, assessing how stable they were with the saw running and our weight over the boards. Finally, we used the jaws or clamps to hold a workpiece in place, prying on the boards to see how well the clamps would hold. We even set up the biscuit joiner to test how well they hold pieces under force.

Between those tests, which replicate what a typical DIYer or contractor might put these workbenches through, we had a good idea of what they could offer.

A portable workbench should be lightweight and durable, and it should have the features to assist with a number of projects. After all, a portable workbench’s most desirable feature should be versatility. Keep the following considerations in mind while shopping for one of these tools.

When shopping for a portable workbench, size and weight are crucial. Most portable workbenches weigh less than 30 pounds, which is a manageable weight for one person. Some workbenches weigh as little as 15 pounds, though 25 to 30 pounds is the most typical weight range.

Some portable workbenches fold flat to between 4 and 7 inches thick to allow for easy transport and storage. When set up, most portable workbenches have worktops that are approximately 30 inches long by 24 inches wide and stand about 30 inches off the ground, but this varies by model.

Portable workbenches should be sturdy enough to endure abuse but also light enough to transport. To achieve this balance, most workbenches are made of a combination of sturdy steel and lightweight ABS plastic or wood. Some portable workbenches feature steel or aluminum legs that provide a sturdy support system with a benchtop of heavy-duty plastic resin or a lighter wood such as bamboo.

When working on a project, a wobbly surface just won’t do, so a portable workbench must be sturdy. Portable workbenches feature wide-set feet with steel or aluminum legs that help provide stability. Look for a portable workbench with feet coated in rubber or some other nonslip material to prevent the bench from sliding.

Most portable workbenches feature integrated clamping systems. While some portable models have entire benchtops that open to clamp large material, others integrate tracks into the worktop to incorporate holding clamps and large 2-inch bar clamps. These clamps are designed to secure large pieces of wood or metal, allowing the user to cut, sand, or fasten materials.

Many portable workbenches include special features to make life easier. For example, some workbenches are designed with molded handles to make transport easier, whereas others may include measurement markings printed or molded onto the worktop surface. Still other models feature extra pockets and drawers for tool storage, while some even have integrated power strips.

Portable workbenches are designed to meet a variety of demands, and versatility is their greatest benefit. Some workbenches may double as workstations for miter saws, while others have the ability to change shape completely, allowing them to function as both a workbench and sawhorse.

Many workbenches allow users to change the worktop’s height by up to 4 inches, which is handy when using the workbench with a table saw or as a support for cutting longer material. Other styles allow users to change the angle of the workbench to use as a fence for cutting.

If you’re wondering which qualities to look for in a workbench, keep reading for some of the most frequently asked questions about the top portable workbenches.

A quality portable workbench should be durable enough to handle the rigors of a home workshop or pro job site. It should have a sturdy base that prevents it from wobbling while you work. It should include clamping features to hold materials securely in place. A portable workbench also should break down in seconds into a shape that’s compact and light enough for one person to manage.

Unlike dining room tables or kitchen counters, no standard workbench height exists. Workbench heights can range from 28 inches to 38 inches. Workbench heights on the high end are suitable for assembling items and to function as outfeed tables for table saws, while lower workbench heights allow for more leverage for such jobs as sanding. If you’re not sure which height you need, use this literal rule of thumb—the benchtop should meet the same level as the knuckle in your thumb when standing with your arms hanging at your sides.

The weight capacity of workbenches varies. Lighter-duty workbenches can handle a weight of around 250 pounds, which is adequate for most home workshops, while a heavy-duty workbench may have a weight capacity as high as 1,000 pounds.

Most portable workbenches use plastic in their design. While this makes them much lighter than a permanent workbench, plastic isn’t as durable as wood or steel. Plus, portable workbenches have movable joints that allow them to collapse, making them weaker than a standard workbench with no moving parts. With that in mind, most portable workbenches should last many years when properly maintained.

#7811. Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The ruling on Section 287(g) agreements overturns an earlier district court decision.

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:

We vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:

We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:

At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law.  Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

NEXT: Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7810. The Safest Way to Shovel Snow, According to Experts

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

The safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home.  Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

Keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer says. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and plan ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

“Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer says. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

#7809. What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”

Drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

Federal Highway Administration, “Questions and Answers About Vehicle Size and Weight” Federal Highway Administration, “Truck Size and Weight Enforcement Technologies, WIM Technology Overview” Federal Highway Administration, “Compliance Comparative Analysis Technical Report, Compliance Effectiveness of Enforcement” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Inspections” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Out-of-Service Criteria”

#7807. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The federal law did not prohibit the basic AR-15 rifle design.

Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004.  The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today."

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v).  So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated.  The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof.  Second, they included certain features, including:

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and

(v) a grenade launcher….  18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

Under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names.  A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

But guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip.  None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design.  Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock.  How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount?  A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could.  Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design.  Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

Manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance.  I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw).  As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994.  The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design.  And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

#7806. If You See a Taco Bell With THIS On It, Here’s What It Means

A strange metal frame on some new Taco Bell restaurants has people wondering if construction crews forgot something. Here's what it's for.

There are certain restaurant chain designs everyone has come to recognize. McDonald’s golden arches. Pizza Hut’s red roof. But what about the open framing on the side of new Taco Bell buildings?

If you haven’t seen the new Taco Bell design, it includes open framing on the second floor on one side. But why? A recent Reddit post sparked plenty of guesses about what the framing was for.

New Taco Bell Building – What’s the Open Framing? by u/Kindly_Blueberry2814 in whatisit

The design seems to be more aesthetic than functional and is part of Taco Bell’s newer restaurant design, known as Kitchen X. It is part of the company’s move away from its older Spanish-style buildings, which featured arches and stucco exteriors.

“That open metal cage on the left is just decorative framing to make the building look sleek and balanced,” one Reddit user commented. “The left side of the restaurant has lower ceilings for storage, coolers, and the drive-thru lane, so they added that hollow steel frame on top to match the height of the main dining room on the right. There are no stairs or deck up there, just standard roof stuff and AC units hidden behind the wall.”

Another commenter agreed, saying, “It’s just an architectural design feature to give visual balance.”

Taco Bell has introduced Kitchen X at select locations across the United States, including new restaurants in Carver and Rochester, Minnesota. However, the exterior can vary between locations, so not every restaurant has the same framing.

Before Reddit users settled on the decorative explanation, they had plenty of other guesses.

“It’s to land the tacocopter,” one Reddit user joked.

“Future terrace dining,” another Reddit user speculated.

The discussion also turned into a debate about Taco Bell’s changing appearance. Some users said they missed the chain’s older buildings with more character, while others shared photos of former locations with more traditional designs.

Whether you love or hate the look, there’s no denying that it’s eye-popping and hard to miss. Which is probably what the company was hoping for when coming up with the new look.

#7805. Cutting Down Your Own Christmas Tree This Year? 9 Things You Should Know First

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Jamie Birdwell-Branson, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 25, 2026 11:50 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

What’s better than a hike through fragrant evergreens with the nip of crisp winter air (and the effort of chopping your own Christmas tree) to bring a flush to your cheeks this holiday season? Whether you’re in a forest or a tree farm, these tips will help you bring home a terrific tannenbaum.

If you plan on heading into the woods to cut down your Christmas tree, first determine whether you need a permit to do so. Call your municipal officials, for a start. Christmas tree permits are available through Recreation.gov—but hurry, because some offices do sell out of permits.

Some people enjoy decking out the home for the holidays right after they’ve cleared the Thanksgiving dishes, or maybe even right after that first pumpkin spice latte of the season. But if you’re decorating a real tree, it’s best to wait. Even trees that are watered regularly get dried out within 3 weeks of cutting, so try to resist the urge to decorate too early.

Unlike the Christmas trees at the local lots, trees on a farm or in the forest don’t necessarily come in predictable 6- or 8-foot sizes. To avoid disappointment, measure the distance from floor to ceiling where you plan to place your tree to make sure you don’t cut down a tree that’s too big for your house. While you’re at it, measure the space in or above your car to make sure you’ll be able to accommodate the tree, and don’t forget to bring twine, bungees, scissors, and anything else you might need to secure the tree in (or on) your car.

Though cutting down your Christmas tree is a fun holiday excursion, you’ll be handling blades or saws, so it’s important to wear appropriate safety attire. Put on a pair of sturdy boots, pack a pair of heavy work gloves. Avoid wearing loose clothing to keep it from tangling in the tools or trees.

DeWalt’s 15-inch hand saw cuts on the push and pull strokes for rapid material removal, and works well at different angles. Read the review.

Depending on where you’re cutting down your tree, there may be restrictions on the tools you can use. Although a chain saw is the quickest and easiest way to fell a tree, many tree farms and national forests don’t allow their use, so be prepared with a handsaw or axe, just in case.

Even if you immediately spot “the one,” it’s best to do a full walk-through before you commit to a particular tree. Christmas tree farms are often arranged by size or type of tree, so taking a look at everything else that’s available will help you avoid buyer’s remorse on the way out to the car.

Try to cut your Christmas tree as low to the ground as you possibly can. This will not only make it a taller tree, but it will also allow another tree to resprout and spread Christmas cheer to future tree-hunters.

Have a partner hold your tree steady to prevent it from falling over before you’ve sawed all the way through the trunk. Also, resist the temptation to push the tree over: Not only is this unsafe, but it will also prevent regrowth.

Your freshly cut Christmas tree will probably be rife with freeloading bugs, sap, and spiderwebs, so give it a good shake before you pack it in the car to keep your living room free of these natural nuisances. Some tree farms even have mechanical shakers that will get the job done, for a fee.

#7804. Second Amendment Roundup, II: Much Ado About Bowie Knives

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Laws on concealed carry are not historical analogues for banning semiautomatic rifles.

In Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment.  If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

A word of caution.  To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife.  Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other.  Any knife can be used for good or bad.  Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns."

No doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are said to have carried them concealed.  But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use.  Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this issue: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

First, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition.  Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban.  "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

Second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36.  "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

These were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans.  "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

Third, the same laws covered handguns.  "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

Where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not.  As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

Fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected.  "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859).  Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens

"[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

#7803. You Can Actually Repair a House in GTA6—But How Realistic Is It?

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a new, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

Yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10

Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10

Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

But still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

#7802. Jonathan Scott’s Trick for Making a Fake Christmas Tree Look Real Is Brilliant

Jonathan Scott shares his favorite Christmas decorating tricks, from making artificial trees look real to refreshing decor without spending more.

There’s no place like home for the holidays. As it gets closer to the most magical time of the year, stores are stocked with decorations big and small, and figuring out how you want your home to look can be a little overwhelming. Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

There’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott says. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”

Even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

Scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a new look out of decorations he already owns.

Those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few new touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most important thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

#7800. Bob Woodward Interviews Justice Kagan, Or Does Justice Kagan Interview Bob Woodward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Kagan sheds some light on her view about leaks, Dobbs, and the Court.

Last month I wrote about an excerpt from Bob Woodward's new book that reveals sources. Most of the sources are deceased, so there is little harm outing them. But Justices Kagan and Breyer are alive and well. Woodward reveals a remarkable conversation with the former. As Woodward would observe, it is less clear that he was interviewing Kagan than Kagan was interviewing him.

"Well, the conclusion of The Brethren was that the center of the court was in control," I said, meaning neither the left nor the right was in charge. "Yes, I prefer it that way," Kagan said. "That's exactly what it should be." That's not the way it is now, I noted. It is not, Kagan confirmed. How did you get such detail in the book? We had time, I said. Of course, it was a different era in which Scott and I were doing the reporting in the late 1970s. I started to tell her about Scott and how he had really discovered the Nixon Tapes because he found Alexander Butterfield. Not letting me off the hook, Kagan asked again, "How did you do it?" Well, we interviewed five sitting justices and 170 law clerks. We got documentation. That's extraordinary, Kagan said. How did you get the documents? The justices must have approved the clerks giving you the documents? I shook my head. Not that we were aware. You make clerks now sign nondisclosure agreements, I noted. "Yes," she said.

Over the years, I've speculated that Justices have authorized their clerks to leak information to the press. The premise of Kagan's questions is that Justices had authorized their clerks to speak with Woodward and Bernstein. But no, the clerks went rogue. If the clerks acted alone in the 1970s, perhaps they did so in 2022 with the Dobbs opinion.

I told her that Brennan and Marshall, the liberal justices on the court, would not help us. Well, who did? Rehnquist and White, I said. Kagan seemed surprised. I recounted the story of calling Justice Lewis Powell at the court one morning and him agreeing to meet. I said when and he said now. "I was in my pajamas, but told him I'd be there in half an hour." You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Justice Kagan clerked for Justice Marshall, who apparently never discussed the sourcing for The Brethren.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I find it odd that Kagan said nothing in response. This is not the sort of statement that could trigger a recusal. She might have said "that debate nearly got my colleague assassinated." But she stayed silent.

I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting."

She mustered a response here, but not to the leak question. Interesting?

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

Kagan likely didn't think she would be quoted.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

No one forced him out. He has life tenure. Instead, Breyer surrendered to the pressure. So much for judicial independence. Justices Alito and Thomas are often charged with being MAGA partisans, but they exhibited robust independence from political forces.

Woodward offers this anecdote about the Thomas confirmation hearing:

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.

I couldn't find any references to other current justices.

I will read the chapters on The Brethren with interest.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures.
