#7758. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

Satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each new matter at the outset?

Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material issues in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or issue. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

Ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

Chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

Satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

Chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same plan from the outset.

Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”

Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

Chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati said earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

Chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be said in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce new technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7757. The Veteran’s Example for America

Veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.

Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.

Across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example shows that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.

The freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.

By defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.

>>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s Greatness

Veterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.

During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.

The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.

Across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.

The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.

Veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Seventy-three percent of veterans cast ballots, compared with 66% of nonveterans.

The index also reports stronger veteran participation in volunteering, in civic organizations and in engagement with public officials and community institutions. Together, these measures point to a broader pattern: For many veterans, military service becomes a lifelong commitment to citizenship, civic responsibility and the preservation of our constitutional republic.

Veterans continue to serve as teachers, business leaders, first responders, elected officials and civic volunteers, bringing military habits of integrity, discipline and teamwork into civilian life. At Military.com, Medal of Honor recipient Clint Romesha captures that enduring impulse, saying, “So many of us veterans just want to continue to serve after service.”

Mr. Romesha identifies teamwork as one of the military’s greatest lessons—“It’s not about me; it’s about the team”—and as a principle that continues to guide veterans long after they leave the uniform behind.

The veteran profiles of “American Heroes: Stories of Service” and “Pledge to Patriots” show this continuing commitment in action. These stories feature veterans mentoring young people, supporting one another, leading nonprofits, responding to disasters and strengthening communities.

>>> Nina and the Bikers

Thousands of veterans serve as poll workers, election officials and observers, helping to administer and safeguard elections. As a former election official and U.S. Navy veteran, I have seen them step forward when communities need poll workers. Through the nonpartisan Vet the Vote initiative, more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers during the 2024 election cycle, up from approximately 63,500 during the 2022 midterms.

National Guard members have supported election operations, security, coordination and emergency response at the request of state authorities. Their commitment to duty, adherence to procedures and record of public service can strengthen confidence in the electoral process they defended in uniform.

On Veterans Day, we honor those who wore the uniform in defense of our nation. We should also follow the example they continue to set—as citizens, poll workers, community leaders and public servants—reminding us that freedoms secured on far-off battlefields must be preserved through faithful participation in self-government at home.

Veterans Day recognizes a profound commitment to country, but it also challenges every American to accept the duties of citizenship.

#7756. Economic Freedom and Educational Opportunity

Education policymakers around the world often overlook a simple formula: To increase educational opportunity, increase economic development.

But to improve development, a country needs the institutions that promote it. That’s why nations that want to help more children succeed should pursue economic freedom.

The latest Economic Freedom of the World report from the Fraser Institute tells the story clearly. The highest-ranked 25% of countries for economic freedom dramatically outperform the lowest-ranked 25%. Incomes are seven times greater, while people work six fewer hours per week. People live 14 years longer. Fewer children die in infancy, and environments are cleaner.

Economic freedom translates into education and economic opportunity. Fewer students in developing nations will drop out in middle school to go to work. More families will be able to afford transportation to school. There will be more opportunities for graduates to get more productive, higher-paying jobs.

>>> Latin America Shifts Toward Market-Oriented Conservatism

Take, for instance, Kurdistan in Iraq, which is focusing more on education now. Iraq ranks 159 out of 165 countries for its legal system and property rights, 152 for size of government, 141 for sound money, 149 for regulation of the economy, and 129 for freedom to trade internationally.

Imagine how many more students in Kurdistan could finish school with a great education if incomes were seven times higher. Imagine the hard trade-offs today that would not be necessary if Iraq were richer.

This point holds worldwide. What would best help a country’s children receive a strong education in the long run? Focus first of all on the country’s economic and legal institutions.

Education is about making plans for society’s future. That means a small government with reliable courts, sound money, secure property rights, and free competition.

Economic development doesn’t automatically mean more government funding for government schools. In many countries, it can mean trusting families with education dollars to choose what is best for their own children.

Indeed, parents are a great education resource. They are the first line of influence to keep their children on track for success, and you don’t even have to pay them a salary.

Governments can do more to consider how to empower parents and teachers. Families know their own children the best. Teachers know their own students as individuals far better than a national government or the United Nations or UNICEF could ever know them.

Using international aid to push an ideological agenda is the wrong policy. Education policy choices should emphasize local knowledge rather than national and international one-size-fits-all, top-down impositions.

>>> Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar and Empower the Developing World

Educators also should teach economic and financial literacy. The scientific evidence is decisive that socialism fails and market economies succeed. We mark Nov. 7 each year as Victims of Communism Day in the United States by remembering the more than 100 million people who died of starvation or were killed under communist and socialist regimes in the 20th century.

On an individual level, each student should be taught the basics of economics and entrepreneurship. These lessons include the fundamentals of human action and incentives, supply and demand, and the invisible hand of Adam Smith. This also includes learning how to be alert to opportunities to create value for others in society while improving one’s own life.

This education means respecting and admiring entrepreneurs. Students should understand why people should be allowed to keep the fruit of their own labor. Students also should understand the value of building capital rather than consumption if they want to prosper.

To prepare students for employment and participation in society, teach economics and inspire entrepreneurship and an entrepreneurial mindset. Then the next generation will better understand the institutional reforms needed to help their country thrive.

Given the results of the latest U.S. election, now that new policymakers with socialist leanings (and actual socialists) will govern in states such as Michigan, New York, California, and elsewhere starting next year, this advice is not just for other countries. It’s also for us. Will we listen?

#7755. New in Civitas Outlook: "Justice Kagan Cries Wolf"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"If Justice Kagan is truly worried about the Court’s declining legitimacy, then she would not accelerate that decline through questioning the legitimacy of her own institution."

My latest essay in Civitas Outlook combines much of my recent thinking about Justice Kagan. She has shifted to different modalities of persuasion over her career on the bench. The latest front is to preemptively blame the Court for destroying democracy and then complain how the Court's legitimacy is being wounded. She is like the arsonist who seeks mercy for burning down her own house. The bigger problem is her predictions are simply wrong. Kagan has some serious crow to eat after the blue tsunami. An entire jurisprudence based on consequentialism fails if the consequences never happen.

Here is the introduction of Justice Kagan Cries Wolf:

Justice Elena Kagan recently confessed, "I'm much better in print than I am in person." She's right. Through a series of carefully coordinated public appearances, Justice Kagan has attempted to influence how her colleagues vote and how the public perceives the Court. Worse still, Kagan made dire predictions about how the Court has wounded democracy and its own legitimacy. But in short order, the midterm elections refuted her consequentialism. Elena Kagan is the Justice who cries wolf. Justices should speak through their judicial writings, not try to distort the process from the sidelines. . . .

This sort of consequentialist judging carries a distinct risk: what if the consequences never manifest? In other words, a jurisprudence based on predicting certain outcomes fails if the predictions are wrong. Kagan did not just try to predict the outcome of the midterm election; she proclaimed she could divine the future of our republic. Alas, in short order, Justice Kagan has proven herself to be less Cook Report and more Miss Cleo.

Kagan's point seems to be that ruling against the President who appoints you is proof you're a fair justice. That premise holds only if the law does not support the appointing President's policy. If a Justice simply rules against the President who appoints him, then the Justice is no longer a judge. In his new book So Ordered, Justice Alito chides so-called "insecure originalists" who favor outcomes that yield results they dislike to bolster a reputation of independence. Alito, "Twenty-first-century originalists should shed this insecure mindset." Yet Kagan intentionally feeds into this insecurity.

Justice Kagan, and all Justices, cannot predict the consequences of their decisions. Chief Justice Roberts can predict a decade-long "long game" no better than Kagan can predict the outcome of a single midterm election. They should stop trying to see into the future. Accordingly, the Justices should not be cowed into altering their rulings based on doomsday predictions of what might happen. As for Justice Kagan, the parable of the girl who cries wolf is on point. She can keep speaking, but we don't have to listen.

My point here echoes my point about the Chief Justice last summer. The conservatives should stop listening to colleagues who do not put the Constitution's best interest at heart.

#7754. The Unexpected Source of Muslim Immigration to France

The ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But foreign observers may be surprised to learn how many of the most recent arrivals came in through the tiny Balkan nation of Slovenia, which enabled a mass migration in 2022-2024. The dynamics of how and why this happened in Europe are well worth our attention in America because, mutatis mutandis, they also obtain along our own southern border. Think of Mexico as our Slovenia.

In 2023, I spent four weeks visiting eight of the countries involved in the transit routes to learn why they had come back to life. What I learned has profound implications for American policy. Led by pioneering member state Hungary, the E.U. had erected a solid barrier along its eastern frontier. But then another member state—Slovenia—elected a liberal government with lax enforcement policies. And that single breach in the defenses left interior countries like France vulnerable once again.

Almost three years have passed since I discovered (and reported) the Slovenia breach in what had been for the previous seven years an effective barrier erected by the European Union. The E.U. effectively put an end to Europe’s catastrophic mass migration crisis of 2014-2016, during which both refugees and terrorists were able to travel freely along the so-called “Balkan Route.”

The Slovenia gap, as I’ll call it, helped flood France with at least 466,000 first-time foreign national asylum and refugee claimants from mostly Muslim-majority nations in 2022-23 alone. Many of these were fast-tracked into the public housing communities now at the center of France’s continuous street violence.

>>> France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes Due

The flow of migrants began in mid-2022 with a key Slovenian election and spiked in 2023 before declining in 2024. Much of the traffic moved along the same Balkan routes traveled by some 800,000 to 900,000 mostly Muslim immigrants during the 2014-2016 crisis, during which there were an estimated two million illegal E.U. border crossings.

The 466,000 migrants who applied for French asylum or refugee status in 2022-23 hailed from places like Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Tunisia, as well as Muslim-majority nations in North Africa. Of those, authorities detected approximately 244,000 who traveled on routes through the Balkans; untold thousands more are believed to have traveled those same routes undetected. Among those who registered were France-bound immigrants like an Afghan I interviewed in a Bosnian migrant camp who was en route to the Slovenia gap.

“Taliban good!” he told me in pidgin English when I asked his opinion about the ruling terrorist group in his home country.

A Breach in the Defenses

The Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.

A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.

E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. When migrants diverted west to avoid it, Austria built another, forcing Slovenia to build a razor-wire fence along the border with Croatia to head off further spillover.

By 2016, the Balkan routes were considered effectively closed. It also helped that the E.U. paid Turkey and some proxy North African nations (and violent militias) billions of euros to stop and block emigration from their territories.

So how did another mass migration start in 2022 that would flood France with tens of thousands more?

In June 2022, Slovenian voters threw out the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party that had built that fence. They elected the center-left Freedom Movement and installed Prime Minister Robert Golob, who had campaigned to tear down Slovenia’s fence and immediately set about doing so.

News Travels Fast

Word spread that a gap in Slovenia’s Balkan route had just opened, so migrants came pouring through it. I toured the forlorn remnants of Slovenia’s fence, observing broken-down sections lying where they had been pushed down. Anyone could walk through at will. I never saw a single police officer as I crossed back and forth repeatedly on foot and by car.

Smugglers and self-directed immigrants (including many from Latin America) quickly figured out they could fly without visas into Serbia for a time, or trek on their own up from Greece and into Bosnia for the onward journey through a narrow sliver of Croatian territory to Slovenia. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.

E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. But with no wall and a porous border, Croatia was effectively unable to oblige. Immigrants on the Bosnia side told me they planned to push for the Slovenia gap and go on to France.

On the U.N.’s Camp Lipa in northwest Bosnia, for instance, nine young men from Morocco and Algeria were hardly worried about Croatian police catching them as they prepared for the short trek across Croatia to the Slovenia border.

“No problem!!!” almost everyone shouted, laughing as they turned and disappeared into the dark forest, chanting, “Inshallah! Inshallah!”—if God wills it.

Earlier this year, Slovenians elected a conservative government that plans to rebuild the fence. But that’s too late for France.

>>> Spain’s Housing Backlash Is a Warning for America

American Slovenias

Of course, though it was the liberal Slovene government that opened the side door into the E.U., it was government policies in destination countries that lured them through. France, the U.K., and other European countries have clung to policies and processes that prevent quick deportations and, at the same time, provide the arrivals with public welfare. These are powerful lures.

In 2023, immigrants told me they knew France and other destination countries wouldn’t—or couldn’t—deport them. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how important the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. This point is very important.”

There’s a lesson for Americans in this practically unknown aspect of French politics: the United States can easily become like France if voters elect liberal politicians who favor lenient immigration policies.

Not just that, though. To avoid becoming France, U.S. policies must include making sure that Mexico and the transit countries of Central America never become the Slovenia I saw a few years ago.

#7753. Free Speech Under Siege in France

The median American read only two books in 2025, and 40% of us read not a single book all year. The French are more literary; they read an average of 18 books a year. They venerate authors—the more intellectual, controversial, and impenetrable the better.

But that doesn’t mean authors are beyond criticism in France. The work of Michel Houellebecq, for example, has long been controversial. In 2002, he was charged with inciting racism for calling Islam “the stupidest religion.” Mosques in Paris and Lyon joined with the World Islamic League to bring the charges against him. Paris judges found him not guilty.

In response, the head of the Mosque of Lyon said, “Islam now can be insulted freely. The permission to insult Islam has now been given.”

Well, yes. That’s how free speech works. Insulting a person, institution, or religion may be unfair, unkind, or even unwise, but in these United States at least, it is not illegal. That’s why we tolerate the views of podcast harpy Jennifer Welch and chief “Groyper” Nick Fuentes, among others.

But France, like Britain and Germany, has no First Amendment. In all three countries, people are routinely arrested for speech that in the United States would be legal.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

Houellebecq’s book “Submission” was published in January 2015, on the same day Islamist terrorists murdered 12 journalists and staff at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo for having republished cartoons depicting the Muslim prophet Mohammed.

“Submission” invokes an imaginary future (2022!) where a Muslim party has won national elections and governs according to Sharia law—among other things, legalizing polygamy. The protagonist, a middle-aged man, eventually decides to convert to Islam so he can have more wives.

Houellebecq took a lot of criticism for the book but was not formally charged. He was raised as a young child in Algeria at the end of its French rule, which ended in a bloody terrorist campaign and war. That experience may have shaped his bleak view of France’s future.

Houellebecq is back under investigation by a judge, this time for comments made in 2022 in an interview with the outlet Front Populaire. The investigation was instigated by a complaint from the Grand Mosque of Paris in 2023 and may result in criminal charges.

Here’s some of what he said. (Translation by The Critic. It sounds better in French):

The wish of the native French population is not that Muslims assimilate but that they stop robbing and assaulting them. Or, another solution, that they leave. … When entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place. There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclans in reverse.

The “great replacement” theory “[is] not a theory, it’s a fact. It’s statistical evidence.”

The first two statements are his opinion. The second is unsavory, especially given the reportedly racially motivated October murder in Paris of a black French national. But it is his prediction, not an incitement to violence.

The third statement, as Houellebecq says, is fact. European populations across the West are shrinking, while foreign peoples immigrate in large numbers. One thus replaces the other. We can discuss whether this is good or bad, or why it happens, but not the undeniable fact that it is occurring.

But whether he is right or wrong is not the issue. The protesters taking to the streets every week in France are motivated by various causes from teacher shortages to pensions to Gaza, not an interview in Front Populaire they never read. I doubt any of the young men in Marseille looting luxury stores for sneakers and bags have read a book, let alone one by Michel Houellebecq.

>>> The Unexpected Source of Muslim Immigration to France

In a recent interview with Ben Shapiro, comedian and writer Rob Schneider said:

When the truth becomes a right-wing concept, then I think you have to stand up for it…It’s going to cost you to speak your opinion. It’s going to cost you jobs, it’s going to cost you money, but it’s going to cost you more if you don’t speak up and you lose this incredible experiment in freedom that we have.

America was founded on free speech, which is the only way to get to the truth. If we lose that, we lose all. France’s revolution followed ours by 13 years. But whereas ours was against an occupying overseas power, theirs was internal and devolved into a purge for ideological purity. Free speech was the very basis of our revolution, but it was an early casualty in theirs.

I was U.S. Consul in Slovakia for three years. Everyone my age there remembered life under communism. The system survived partly because of the Soviet Union’s threat of military force, which they used in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 to suppress popular uprisings. But Czechoslovakia and the other Soviet satellite states also had repressive police, informers, and political prisons to keep people down.

People shared bitter jokes, such as “we pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us,” about socialist economics. They listened to jazz, which was subversive without words. They listened to Voice of America and read books in secret. But they knew better than to speak out freely against the communist system unless they were prepared for the gulag or death. That’s why it lasted almost 50 years.

If convicted, Houellebecq could face up to a year in prison and heavy fines. But behind bars with him would go France’s freedom of speech. We watch from America as our oldest ally—along with Britain, Germany, and others—goes down this well-worn path to authoritarian censorship. Whatever happens there, we need to hold fast to our principles here:

“Congress shall make no law…abridging the freedom of speech…”

#7752. Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

There is not much new information revealed beyond what is in The Brethren, but we learn how Woodward obtained the information.

Bob Woodward's new book is a bit unusual. There is no coherent narrative or flow. Each chapter simply tells the story of another one of his sources. Chapters 36 through 43 walk through his interviews with Supreme Court Justices, law clerks, and others for The Brethren. The book is a collection of his recollections, mostly from recorded memos, and what all of his source said.

Beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak. He invariably starts by finding someone low on the totem pole, building trust, and working his way up.

Scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country. The names of all the law clerks, past and present, was readily available public information. I cannot underscore enough how important it is in journalism to focus on the low end of the totem pole. Presidents, justices, cabinet officials are all important interviews.

What began as a somewhat random "catch-as-catch-can" for Scott and me helped us get inside, as we used what we collected to dig deeper. Quoting information or documents we already possessed helped give confidence to other clerks who would then sometimes reach into their own archives to add details and documents. . .  .

Most of the information in our book, The Brethren, is based on interviews with more than 200 people, including five justices who talked, 170 former and current law clerks, and several dozen former employees of the court. Virtually all the interviews were conducted on deep background, meaning that the identity of the sources would be kept confidential for their lifetimes but all the information could be used in the book. Since all of the justices are now deceased, I am lifting the lid on our interviews with them.

This sort of journalism takes time and time and more time. But eventually, he has enough information that principals feel comfortable talking to him. And even if he learned what happened from multiple sources, asking yet another source opens up the possibility for even more insights to be gleaned.

Chapter 36 recounts Woodward's interactions with Justice Stewart, who invited the reporter to his home for an interview. Stewart spoke very critically of Chief Justice Burger. That interview convinced Woodward there was enough to write a book. The publisher gave him and Scott Armstrong a $300,000 advance. That is more than $1.5 million in present-day value.

Chapter 37 recounts Woodward's interview with Justice Powell. Powell invited him to the Court—right away. Woodward arrived at 4:30 p.m. that day. Powell said, "Intellectually there is no Brandeis or Frankfurter or Cardozo on the court now." I've made similar comments since Justice Scalia's passing. I wonder if any members of the current Court think they are at the intellectual level of Holmes or Story? I appreciate Powell's humility.

Woodward would interview Powell two more times. I found these comments about Roe striking:

I asked him about the Supreme Court's landmark 1973 abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton, which legalized abortion nationwide. "It was hard for me and I was frankly strongly result oriented," Powell said of the decision. "I would support abortion funding by the states if I was in the legislature," he added. This caught me off-guard and seemed contrary to the opinions he had written saying there was no right to a state-funded abortion.

"I thought the abortion laws were atrocious," Powell continued, referring to the state abortion laws prohibiting abortion. "If you wanted to pay for an abortion you could get one." I noted his selection of the word "wanted" instead of "could afford" which was a big part of the issue as I saw it.

There should be no doubt that Roe was an outcome-driven decision. There was no law—just policy.

Chapter 38 focuses on how he interviewed more than 170 law clerks. Powell authorized his law clerks to speak to Woodward. Burger's former clerks were "at times the most helpful," especially since Woodward never bothered asking Burger to speak. I already recounted the story in which he "borrowed" Justice Brennan's history of the Watergate tape case.

Chapter 39 explains how Justice Powell thought the Justices should talk to reporters to minimize the bad press. Powell wrote in a draft letter to Burger that he never sent: "I had rather someone on the Court discussed this with him accurately than leave him to reach his own conclusions with the right to say that he was stonewalled by the Justices."

Chapter 40 discusses Armstrong's interview with Justice Blackmun, and the resulting "19-page single-spaced memo." There were a few useful nuggets. Blackmun appreciated how he wasn't Nixon's first or even second choice for the seat.

"I am humbled by the fact that I was number three, not the number one choice," Blackmun said of his appointment to the Supreme Court. Nixon's first choice, Clement Haynsworth, a federal judge from South Carolina, and second choice, G. Harrold Carswell, a federal judge from Florida, were rejected narrowly in brutal public fights, largely over concerns that Nixon was attempting to shift the court's ideology, which of course he was. Blackmun had been confirmed unanimously in May 1970 in a 94-to-0 vote. "A scarecrow could get nominated after what had happened," Blackmun continued. "It was a difficult period for the Senate. A number of [senators] told me that they wanted to get it over with. They had a real sense of relief that an average guy had come along with whom they couldn't find much wrong."

I wonder if Justice Kennedy ever had similar marks of humility, as a fellow third-choice?

Blackmun was also assigned the Roe opinion because Chief didn't want to take the heat:

Blackmun said he was well aware that no matter what he wrote, the opinion would be controversial and he would be hated and vilified. The chief could not afford to take on such a controversial case himself, particularly from the minority. "That's why I was assigned the abortion memo. We were scattered on it," Blackmun said. Douglas was the court's mischievous liberal, the rebel, and couldn't be the author. Any abortion opinion Douglas wrote would be widely questioned outside the court. Brennan was a firm vote for striking down the state abortion laws, but he was the court's only sitting Catholic. As such, Brennan could not be expected to take the heat from the Catholic anti-abortion groups. Marshall could not author for similar reasons: An opinion by the court's only Black man could be perceived as specifically designed for Black people or incite race-fueled blame for the decision. Stewart would have trouble going very far… That left one option: Blackmun.

By Chapter 41, the first draft of the book was complete. Now, Powell declined to talk further with Woodward.

Chapter 42 recounts a fairly gruff interview with Justice White, who gave up virtually nothing.

Chapter 43 relays how Justice Powell wrote to Chief Justice Burger about the new book. Powell, of course, did not disclose how he spoke with Woodward, and how he authorized his clerks to do the same. I can get Burger's frustration.

Chief Justice Warren Burger erupted in a letter back to Powell, squarely blaming the clerks and noting "there are hazards in talking with certain 'categories' in this life"—meaning me and Scott, or reporters in general. He criticized the clerks for seeming to have succumbed to the "glamour" of rubbing shoulders with "print names!" . . .

I wondered if Burger knew that five of the seven justices in his ranks had talked to us and several had given their clerks permission to assist us.

If only Burger knew that Powell and others blabbed. I suspect Chief Justice Roberts can relate.

It also turns out that Woodward asked a young Stephen Breyer to fact-check the book.

Another secret that has a certain historic value today was that one weekend before The Brethren went to the printers, a young man named Stephen Breyer came over to my home. He sat in the living room and read the book cover to cover. At that time he was chief counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee chaired by Senator Ted Kennedy. Scott had insisted we have the book's use of legal terms checked for obvious errors. After reading, Breyer told us it was "a hell of a book."

I would note there is no discussion of interviewing Justice Rehnquist, even though Rehnquist is named as a source. Something is off.

That's it. Nothing earth-shattering. But it is a shame Woodward decided to relay non-public communications with Breyer and Kagan, who are both alive and well.

NEXT: New in Civitas Outlook: "Justice Kagan Cries Wolf"

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7751. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7750. The Wages of War

Consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock

Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary

That’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

That’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

#7749. New Jersey’s “Islamophobia” Bill Is a Blasphemy Law in Disguise

New Jersey legislators are considering a bill that would be the first in the nation to define “Islamophobia.” It’s not merely descriptive, however. It is so overbroad that it would make it all but impossible to evaluate Islam and the culture it produces in any meaningful way.

That is because a provision in it mandates that public officials and law enforcement officers use the bill’s definitions when considering whether a civil or criminal law has been violated.

It is sure to run into American protections for free speech that are unusually strong even by Western standards. Adherents of every religion have learned over the centuries that hearing their faith smeared, even irrationally (Islamophobia means “an irrational fear of Islam”), is a price they want to pay.

The bill comes as the election of several Muslims to political office nationwide has refocused attention on the nature of Islam and especially its political dimension, or Islamism.

Television scenes of Muslim youth ransacking stores, government offices, and national symbols in France and throughout Europe have also drawn attention to the capacity, or even willingness, of Western societies to assimilate immigrants from the Muslim world. A political alliance between Islamism and the Left is another factor often discussed.

The New Jersey bill, A1146, is moreover championed by the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a pressure group devoted to increasing the number of Muslim elected officials, but which has been declared a “foreign terrorist organization” in Texas and Florida because of its association with the Muslim Brotherhood.

>>> Free Speech Under Siege in France

All of this puts A1146 in the crossroads of a volatile debate growing in America and around the world—a debate which A1146 seems expressly made to shut down.

The clause at the very end of the bill requiring that the definitions be used in investigations makes clear that what is at hand is not merely an exercise in informing the citizenry about what constitutes Islamophobia (already a loaded term). It says in full that:

In reviewing, investigating, or deciding whether there has been a violation of any policy, law, or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts under the civil or criminal laws of this State, a public official or law enforcement officer shall take into consideration the definition of Islamophobia contained in subsection a. of this section for the purposes of determining whether the alleged act was motivated by Islamophobia and discriminatory anti-Muslim intent.

Subsection A has 13 different definitions that would catch in its nettle now viewed as legitimate. It starts by asserting that Islamophobia includes “hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture.”

The second would also chill debate, saying that Islamophobia includes “hostility and fear of Islam, and as a result, a fear of and aversion to all Muslims or the majority of Muslims.”

Same for No. 5, which includes “making mendacious, dehumanizing, demonizing, or stereotypical allegations about Muslims, or of Muslims as a collective group.”

No. 11 carries no small degree of irony with regard to the Garden State. It stipulates that Islamophobia includes “accusing Muslim citizens of being more loyal to a transnational Muslim community or to their countries of origin, or to the alleged priorities of Muslims worldwide, than to the interests of the people of New Jersey or the interests of the people of the United States.”

#7748. After Weil Gotshal’s collapse, law firm merger interest heats up

Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock)

The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

“Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”

“A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

“The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

“We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”

#7747. AFT Boss Randi Weingarten’s Sleazy Book Scam Keeps Growing—and Teachers Paid for It All

Becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

And the new documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

Outside consultants, a New York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target

The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

The new form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

On Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

The new filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability company controlled by Weingarten.

That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled company to $205,000.

And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

The union says the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

The minority can still request materials and issue reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine

The new 2026 filing supplies further evidence that any ongoing review should examine: The additional royalty payment, the fresh publication expense routed to the literary agent, the large PR contract and the further $591,174 to Patterson Belknap all post-date the period covered by the prior report.

Payments to the Weingarten-controlled entity, the literary agent, the PR firm and the consultants raise questions about whether dues money collected from teachers was used for the personal benefit of the union’s top officer.

Federal labor filings exist precisely so that members and the public can review such expenditures.

When these records show repeated transfers linked to an officer’s private project, the disclosures themselves supply the basis for scrutiny.

Teachers who don’t want their hard-earned paychecks to underwrite an officer’s vanity project have a practical alternative.

Organizations such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance offer membership—including free liability insurance—without routing teacher dues to electoral campaigns or left-wing causes.

If enough fed-up teachers leave the AFT, people like Randi Weingarten might think twice about wasting members’ money on personal and political pet projects.
